A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UPLiFT work. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable matching of retained, revised, and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original segmentation, depth-estimation, generative-task, efficiency, and ablation results, including Tables 1–8 and appendix visualizations.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds fast-mode evaluations, architectural ablations, convolutional-backbone results, and qualitative comparisons.

M1.justification: v2 introduces UPLiFTFAST inference execution through BatchNorm folding, channels-last layout, a fused Triton Local Attender kernel, and graph compilation (Section 3.4, Appendix A.5). The architecture and training objective remain unchanged. Algorithm 1 documents the existing Local Attender rather than introducing another operator.

E1.justification: The training datasets and evaluated tasks and datasets are retained. New ResNet-50 and ConvNeXt-S evaluations use the existing COCO/VOC segmentation coverage; their pretraining-corpus descriptions identify backbone configurations rather than newly conducted dataset experiments.

E2.justification: v2 adds AnyUp-v2 to the main predictive and efficiency comparisons, its chunked variant to the scaling study, and NATTEN-based windowed cross-attention alternatives in Table 9. These introduce efficient local-attention comparators important to the central efficiency argument. The original AnyUp remains as AnyUp-v1.

E3.justification: New evaluations vary encoder/decoder widths, remove the encoder, test windowed attention with 1/4/8/12 heads and 5×5 windows, and add convolutional backbones and fast-mode execution. The efficiency study replaces the 48-GB A6000 with an 80-GB H100 alongside the retained A5000, and tests AnyUp-v2 chunk size 10. Existing main-benchmark training and metrics are retained.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained training-depth, neighborhood, and VAE ablations, v2 adds encoder/decoder capacity and encoder-removal tests (Table 8), Local Attender versus windowed-attention tests (Table 9), and multi-baseline PCA case studies (Figure 9). The efficiency analysis also expands to examine fast-mode and chunking tradeoffs.

E5.justification: Both versions report point-estimate task scores and averaged latencies. Appendix B.2 retains three warm-up batches followed by averaging ten measurement batches. No new seed counts, repeated-training-run information, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported.

E6.justification: Table 1 adds AnyUp-v2 and UPLiFTFAST results. Under the retained 448×448/A5000 setting, FAST reports 41.6 ms versus regular UPLiFT's 79.4 ms, with VOC mIoU 85.08 versus 85.21. Tables 8–10 add architectural and convolutional-backbone results; scaling curves and qualitative findings also expand. Original generative and DINOv3 scores are retained. H100 results replace A6000 results, preventing a same-hardware comparison there.

T1.justification: The Local Attender definitions, O(nT) scaling argument, and training equations (1)–(5) are unchanged. Algorithm 1 restates the existing operations as pseudocode; no new theorem, proof, formal assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: efficient iterative pixel-dense upsampling, semantic consistency through Local Attender, strong predictive performance, and competitive generative upsampling. Additional experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 qualifies the efficiency interpretation by acknowledging AnyUp-v2's linear scaling and memory advantages over regular UPLiFT. It adds a stronger-inductive-bias hypothesis for Local Attender, capacity and chunking tradeoffs, and explanations of smoothness, feature bleed, and background artifacts. Appendix D.3 also cautions that visually cleaner features do not necessarily improve downstream performance.

D1.justification: v2 adds detailed tensor-shape and broadcasting pseudocode, specifies the encoder's ten and decoder's six convolutional layers, explains the fast-mode implementation, and reports approximately nine hours of UPLiFT training on one A5000. It also adds code/configuration access guidance. These substantially expand reproducibility information without establishing changes to the original training procedure.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Neighborhood Attention Transformer and Segment Anything. Section 2.1 distinguishes Local Attender from AnyUp-v2/NATTEN, while the appendix discusses SAM supervision in LoftUp. The broader related-work structure and existing citations are retained.

P1.justification: Editorial changes are localized: Section 3.2 is shortened, wording and typographical errors are corrected, Section 3.4 is added, and Appendix A gains numbered subsections. The main narrative and section order remain largely intact; most expansion documents new experiments or technical details.

P2.justification: Figures 3–5 are redrawn with clearer feature visualizations, labels, and scale relationships. v2 adds Algorithm 1, Tables 8–10, and the PCA comparison in Figure 9. Efficiency plots receive additional curves, wider axes, and revised hardware panels; Table 1 gains rows. Retained appendix exhibits are also relocated and renumbered.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for the central efficiency and Local Attender claims through efficient AnyUp-v2 comparisons, controlled windowed-attention and capacity ablations, and fast-mode speed/accuracy evaluation. The pseudocode and architecture details address important reproducibility gaps in v1. These gains outweigh a limited reporting regression: Table 1's unchanged 'second best' depth-accuracy caption conflicts with the added AnyUp-v2 results.
